Session 1 · about 10 min

The A/D converter block diagram

Asked: “Draw the block diagram of an analog-to-digital converter.” F17

Picture

The idea

An analog signal xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) has a value at every instant, and that value can be any real number. A computer can store neither, so the converter fixes them one at a time.

  • Sampler. It reads the signal once every TTT seconds and keeps only those values: x(n)=xa(nT)x(n) = x_a(nT)x(n)=xa​(nT). The sampling rate is Fs=1/TF_s = 1/TFs​=1/T samples per second. After this step time is discrete, but each value can still be any real number.
  • Quantizer. It replaces each sample by the nearest of a fixed set of allowed levels, which gives xq(n)x_q(n)xq​(n). Now the amplitude is discrete too. The small difference eq(n)=xq(n)−x(n)e_q(n) = x_q(n) - x(n)eq​(n)=xq​(n)−x(n) is the quantization error, and it is lost for good.
  • Coder. It writes each level as a binary number. With LLL levels it needs bbb bits per sample, where 2b≥L2^b \ge L2b≥L.

Real converters add two helpers. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter goes in front of the sampler so that no frequency above Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2 gets in (Session 3), and a sample-and-hold circuit keeps each sample still while the quantizer and coder work on it (Session 2).

Write this in the exam

Draw xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) → [Sampler] → x(n)x(n)x(n) → [Quantizer] → xq(n)x_q(n)xq​(n) → [Coder] → 0 1 0 1 1 …, with the three blocks inside a dashed box labelled “A/D converter”. Then explain the blocks:

  1. Sampling converts the continuous-time signal into a discrete-time signal by taking its value at the instants t=nTt = nTt=nT: x(n)=xa(nT)x(n) = x_a(nT)x(n)=xa​(nT), where TTT is the sampling interval and Fs=1/TF_s = 1/TFs​=1/T is the sampling rate.
  2. Quantization converts the discrete-time, continuous-valued signal into a discrete-time, discrete-valued (digital) signal. Each sample is rounded or truncated to one of a finite set of levels. The difference eq(n)=xq(n)−x(n)e_q(n) = x_q(n) - x(n)eq​(n)=xq​(n)−x(n) is the quantization error.
  3. Coding represents each quantized value xq(n)x_q(n)xq​(n) by a bbb-bit binary sequence.

Sampling is always done before quantization. In practice an anti-aliasing low-pass filter precedes the sampler, and the sampling is done by a sample-and-hold circuit.

Check yourself

1. Which signal in the chain is discrete in time but still continuous in amplitude?

x(n)x(n)x(n), the output of the sampler. The quantizer is the block that makes the amplitude discrete.

2. Which step throws information away for good, even in a perfect converter?

Quantization. Sampling loses nothing when Fs>2FmaxF_s > 2F_{max}Fs​>2Fmax​, because the signal can be rebuilt exactly from its samples. The rounding done by the quantizer cannot be undone.

3. The quantizer has 16 levels. How many bits per sample does the coder send?

4 bits, because 24=162^4 = 1624=16.

Session 2 · about 12 min

Sampling with an ideal sample-and-hold circuit

Asked: “Explain sampling using an ideal sample-and-hold circuit.” F17

Picture

The idea

The quantizer and coder need a little time to finish one conversion. If the input kept changing during that time, the converter would be measuring a moving target. The sample-and-hold (S/H) circuit fixes this: it grabs the voltage at the sampling instant and keeps it frozen until the conversion is finished.

  • Parts. An input buffer amplifier, an electronic switch, a hold capacitor CCC, and an output buffer amplifier. A clock running at FsF_sFs​ opens and closes the switch.
  • Sample (track) mode. The switch is closed. The capacitor charges through it, so the capacitor voltage follows the input xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t).
  • Hold mode. At the sampling instant t=nTt = nTt=nT the switch opens. The capacitor now has nowhere to discharge, because the output buffer draws almost no current, so it keeps the voltage xa(nT)x_a(nT)xa​(nT) steady. The A/D converter quantizes and codes this steady value.
  • Then the switch closes again, the capacitor catches up with the input, and at t=(n+1)Tt = (n+1)Tt=(n+1)T the next value is held. One sample is taken every TTT seconds.

What “ideal” adds. A real S/H needs a short time to catch up with the input (acquisition time). While holding, its voltage slowly sags as charge leaks away (droop). And the exact moment the switch opens wobbles slightly (aperture jitter). An ideal S/H has none of these: it switches instantly, holds a perfectly flat voltage, and adds no noise. Its held values are then exactly xa(nT)x_a(nT)xa​(nT), so it behaves like the ideal sampler x(n)=xa(nT)x(n) = x_a(nT)x(n)=xa​(nT) and adds no distortion.

Write this in the exam

Draw the circuit (buffer → switch → capacitor to ground → buffer, with the switch driven by the sampling clock) and the timing sketch (an input curve, and an output that tracks it and then stays flat). Then write:

In practice, sampling is done by a sample-and-hold circuit, a digitally controlled analog circuit with two modes. In the sample (track) mode the switch is closed and the capacitor voltage follows the input xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t). At the sampling instant t=nTt = nTt=nT the circuit switches to the hold mode: the switch opens and the capacitor holds the value xa(nT)x_a(nT)xa​(nT) constant for as long as the A/D converter needs to quantize and code it. This repeats every T=1/FsT = 1/F_sT=1/Fs​ seconds, so the output samples are x(n)=xa(nT)x(n) = x_a(nT)x(n)=xa​(nT) for −∞<n<∞-\infty < n < \infty−∞<n<∞.

An ideal S/H has zero acquisition time, no droop during the hold, and no aperture uncertainty, so the held value is exactly xa(nT)x_a(nT)xa​(nT). It introduces no distortion and is equivalent to an ideal sampler. To avoid aliasing, FsF_sFs​ must be greater than 2Fmax2F_{max}2Fmax​.

Check yourself

1. Why can the A/D converter not quantize the input directly, without the S/H?

The input keeps changing while the converter works, so different bits of the code would be decided at different input values, and the code would be wrong. The S/H keeps the value still until the conversion is done.

2. What is droop, and how much of it does an ideal S/H have?

Droop is the held voltage sagging slowly because the capacitor leaks charge. An ideal S/H has none.

3. In the timing sketch, which mode is the circuit in when the green line is flat?

Hold mode: the switch is open.

Session 3 · about 15 min

The spectrum of a sampled signal, and what happens if Fs<2FmaxF_s < 2F_{max}Fs​<2Fmax​

Asked: “Spectrum relation X(F)=∑k=−∞∞Xa(F−kFs)X(F) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X_a(F - kF_s)X(F)=∑k=−∞∞​Xa​(F−kFs​); what happens if Fs<2FmaxF_s < 2F_{max}Fs​<2Fmax​?” F17

Picture

The idea

Sampling in time makes the spectrum repeat in frequency. The spectrum of the samples is the analog spectrum copied and shifted to 0,±Fs,±2Fs,…0, \pm F_s, \pm 2F_s, \dots0,±Fs​,±2Fs​,…, with all the copies added together:

X(F)=Fs∑k=−∞∞Xa(F−kFs)X(F) = F_s \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X_a(F - kF_s)X(F)=Fs​k=−∞∑∞​Xa​(F−kFs​)

The question prints this without the FsF_sFs​ in front, but Proakis has it. It only scales the height, so everything below holds either way.

Suppose xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) is band-limited, which means Xa(F)=0X_a(F) = 0Xa​(F)=0 for ∣F∣>Fmax\lvert F \rvert > F_{max}∣F∣>Fmax​. Each copy is then 2Fmax2F_{max}2Fmax​ wide, and neighbouring copies sit FsF_sFs​ apart. The original copy ends at FmaxF_{max}Fmax​, and the next copy starts at Fs−FmaxF_s - F_{max}Fs​−Fmax​.

  • When Fs≥2FmaxF_s \ge 2F_{max}Fs​≥2Fmax​, the next copy starts after the original ends, so the copies do not overlap (picture b). In the band ∣F∣≤Fs/2\lvert F \rvert \le F_s/2∣F∣≤Fs​/2 the spectrum is just FsXa(F)F_s X_a(F)Fs​Xa​(F), so an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2 gives back xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) exactly. This is the sampling theorem. (Session 9 shows why the theorem asks for Fs>2FmaxF_s > 2F_{max}Fs​>2Fmax​, strictly greater.)
  • When Fs<2FmaxF_s < 2F_{max}Fs​<2Fmax​, the copies overlap (picture c), and where they overlap their tails add together. High frequencies from the neighbouring copies land on top of the low frequencies of the original. This is aliasing. The spectrum in ∣F∣≤Fs/2\lvert F \rvert \le F_s/2∣F∣≤Fs​/2 no longer has the shape of Xa(F)X_a(F)Xa​(F), so no filter can recover xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t).

The same thing seen in time: a frequency above Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2 disguises itself as a lower one. Sampled at 10 Hz, a 7 Hz cosine gives exactly the same samples as a 3 Hz cosine, because 7−10=−37 - 10 = -37−10=−3, and a cosine does not care about the sign of its frequency.

Write this in the exam

The spectrum of the sampled signal is the analog spectrum repeated periodically with period FsF_sFs​:

X(F)=Fs∑k=−∞∞Xa(F−kFs)X(F) = F_s \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X_a(F - kF_s)X(F)=Fs​k=−∞∑∞​Xa​(F−kFs​)

[Draw pictures (a) and (b), and (c) for the second part.] If xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) is band-limited to FmaxF_{max}Fmax​ and Fs≥2FmaxF_s \ge 2F_{max}Fs​≥2Fmax​, the copies do not overlap, so X(F)=FsXa(F)X(F) = F_s X_a(F)X(F)=Fs​Xa​(F) for ∣F∣≤Fs/2\lvert F \rvert \le F_s/2∣F∣≤Fs​/2, and xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) can be recovered with an ideal low-pass filter.

If Fs<2FmaxF_s < 2F_{max}Fs​<2Fmax​, the shifted copies overlap. Frequency components above the folding frequency Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2 fold back into the band ∣F∣≤Fs/2\lvert F \rvert \le F_s/2∣F∣≤Fs​/2 and add to the components already there. This is called aliasing. The spectrum of the original signal is distorted, and xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) cannot be recovered from its samples. A frequency F0F_0F0​ shows up as its alias F0−kFsF_0 - kF_sF0​−kFs​, the one that lies inside ∣F∣≤Fs/2\lvert F \rvert \le F_s/2∣F∣≤Fs​/2. To avoid aliasing, choose Fs>2FmaxF_s > 2F_{max}Fs​>2Fmax​ (the Nyquist rate is 2Fmax2F_{max}2Fmax​), or band-limit the signal with an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before sampling.

Check yourself

1. Audio containing a 4 kHz tone is sampled at 6 kHz. Where does the tone appear?

At 4−6=−24 - 6 = -24−6=−2 kHz, which you hear as a 2 kHz tone.

2. What is the folding frequency when Fs=6F_s = 6Fs​=6 kHz?

Fs/2=3F_s/2 = 3Fs​/2=3 kHz.

3. Which filter prevents aliasing, and where does it go?

An anti-aliasing low-pass filter with cutoff at most Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2, placed before the sampler. Once aliasing has happened, no filter can undo it.

Session 4 · about 15 min · ★ asked three times

Quantizing a sinusoid with a midtread quantizer, and reducing the error

Asked: “Graphically illustrate quantization of a sinusoid (midtread quantizer); how to reduce quantization error?” F14F17TT1

Picture

The idea

The quantizer has a ladder of allowed levels spaced Δ\DeltaΔ apart. Δ\DeltaΔ is called the step size, or the resolution. Each sample is moved onto a rung of the ladder. With rounding it goes to the nearest rung, so it never moves by more than half a step:

eq(n)=xq(n)−x(n)e_q(n) = x_q(n) - x(n)eq​(n)=xq​(n)−x(n) −Δ2≤eq(n)≤Δ2-\frac{\Delta}{2} \le e_q(n) \le \frac{\Delta}{2}−2Δ​≤eq​(n)≤2Δ​

In the picture the levels are 0,±Δ,±2Δ,±3Δ0, \pm\Delta, \pm 2\Delta, \pm 3\Delta0,±Δ,±2Δ,±3Δ. Every red bar is shorter than half a step, and the bottom strip shows the same errors as a sequence, all inside the ±Δ/2\pm\Delta/2±Δ/2 band.

Midtread or midrise. Plot the output level against the input and you get a staircase. If zero is one of the levels, the staircase has a flat step (a “tread”) running through the origin, and the quantizer is called midtread. Any input with ∣x∣<Δ/2\lvert x \rvert < \Delta/2∣x∣<Δ/2 comes out as exactly 0, so silence stays silent. If the origin sits on a vertical edge (a “riser”) instead, the quantizer is midrise. Its levels are ±Δ/2,±3Δ/2,…\pm\Delta/2, \pm 3\Delta/2, \dots±Δ/2,±3Δ/2,…, and it never outputs 0.

For a sinusoid, the error between two levels rises like a sawtooth from −Δ/2-\Delta/2−Δ/2 to +Δ/2+\Delta/2+Δ/2. Its average power is

Pq=Δ212P_q = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}Pq​=12Δ2​

so the error power depends only on the step size. Halve Δ\DeltaΔ and the error power falls to a quarter.

How to reduce the quantization error

  1. Use a smaller step Δ\DeltaΔ, which means more levels and more bits. Since Δ=(xmax−xmin)/(L−1)\Delta = (x_{max} - x_{min})/(L-1)Δ=(xmax​−xmin​)/(L−1), each extra bit doubles LLL and roughly halves Δ\DeltaΔ. That cuts PqP_qPq​ to a quarter and raises the SQNR by about 6 dB.
  2. Round instead of truncating. Truncation always chops the sample down to the level below, so the error can be almost a whole Δ\DeltaΔ. Rounding keeps it within ±Δ/2\pm\Delta/2±Δ/2.
  3. Match the quantizer’s range to the signal. Scale the input so it uses all the levels but never goes past the top or bottom one. Beyond the ends the quantizer clips, and that error is far bigger than Δ/2\Delta/2Δ/2.
  4. Use non-uniform quantization (companding), such as the μ-law and A-law used for speech. The levels are close together near zero, where the signal spends most of its time, and further apart for large values.

Write this in the exam

Draw the figure: the sinusoid; horizontal lines Δ\DeltaΔ apart for the allowed levels, with one level at 0 (midtread); vertical lines at the sampling instants; each sample moved to the nearest level (dots on the grid). Underneath, sketch the error eq(n)=xq(n)−x(n)e_q(n) = x_q(n) - x(n)eq​(n)=xq​(n)−x(n), which stays between −Δ/2-\Delta/2−Δ/2 and +Δ/2+\Delta/2+Δ/2. Then write:

Quantization converts each sample of continuous amplitude into one of a finite set of levels spaced Δ\DeltaΔ apart. A midtread quantizer has zero as one of its output levels. With rounding, the quantization error is bounded by ∣eq(n)∣≤Δ/2\lvert e_q(n) \rvert \le \Delta/2∣eq​(n)∣≤Δ/2, and its average power is Pq=Δ2/12P_q = \Delta^2/12Pq​=Δ2/12.

To reduce the quantization error: reduce the step size Δ\DeltaΔ by increasing the number of levels (the number of bits bbb); use rounding rather than truncation; scale the signal to fill the quantizer’s range without overload; or use non-uniform quantization (companding).

import numpy as np
n = np.arange(16)
# the samples x(n)
x = 3*np.sin(2*np.pi*n/16)
# step size (Delta)
D = 1
# midtread: round to nearest level
xq = D*np.round(x/D)
# every error is in [-0.5, 0.5]
print(np.round(xq - x, 3))

Check yourself

1. With Δ=0.2\Delta = 0.2Δ=0.2 and rounding, what is the largest possible quantization error?

0.1, which is half a step.

2. An input of 0.3Δ0.3\Delta0.3Δ goes into a midtread and into a midrise quantizer. What comes out of each?

Midtread: 0, because 0.3Δ0.3\Delta0.3Δ is nearer to 0 than to Δ\DeltaΔ. Midrise: +Δ/2+\Delta/2+Δ/2, its smallest positive level.

3. You double the number of levels over the same range. What happens to PqP_qPq​?

Δ\DeltaΔ roughly halves, so Pq=Δ2/12P_q = \Delta^2/12Pq​=Δ2/12 falls to about a quarter, which is about 6 dB less noise.

Session 5 · about 10 min · ★ asked twice

How many bits for x(n)=6.35cos⁡(πn/10)x(n) = 6.35\cos(\pi n/10)x(n)=6.35cos(πn/10)?

Asked: “The DT signal x(n)=6.35cos⁡(π/10)nx(n) = 6.35\cos(\pi/10)nx(n)=6.35cos(π/10)n is quantized with a resolution Δ=0.1\Delta = 0.1Δ=0.1 (also Δ=0.02\Delta = 0.02Δ=0.02). How many bits are needed in the A/D converter?” F21TT1

Picture

The idea

The levels run from the smallest value of the signal to the largest, Δ\DeltaΔ apart. The range divided by Δ\DeltaΔ counts the gaps, and the number of levels is one more than that:

Δ=xmax−xminL−1\Delta = \frac{x_{max} - x_{min}}{L - 1}Δ=L−1xmax​−xmin​​

Turned around, that gives the number of levels:

L=1+xmax−xminΔL = 1 + \frac{x_{max} - x_{min}}{\Delta}L=1+Δxmax​−xmin​​

A bbb-bit code can label 2b2^b2b different levels, so you need the smallest bbb with 2b≥L2^b \ge L2b≥L, that is b=⌈log⁡2L⌉b = \lceil \log_2 L \rceilb=⌈log2​L⌉.

The cos⁡(πn/10)\cos(\pi n/10)cos(πn/10) part matters for only one thing: it really does swing all the way from +1+1+1 (at n=0n = 0n=0) to −1-1−1 (at n=10n = 10n=10). So the signal runs from +6.35+6.35+6.35 down to −6.35-6.35−6.35.

Write this in the exam

Since −1≤cos⁡(πn/10)≤1-1 \le \cos(\pi n/10) \le 1−1≤cos(πn/10)≤1, with both ends reached, xmax=6.35x_{max} = 6.35xmax​=6.35 and xmin=−6.35x_{min} = -6.35xmin​=−6.35.

Range=xmax−xmin=6.35−(−6.35)=12.7\begin{aligned} \text{Range} &= x_{max} - x_{min} \\ &= 6.35 - (-6.35) = 12.7 \end{aligned}Range​=xmax​−xmin​=6.35−(−6.35)=12.7​

Number of levels: L=1+RangeΔL = 1 + \dfrac{\text{Range}}{\Delta}L=1+ΔRange​, and the number of bits is b=⌈log⁡2L⌉b = \lceil \log_2 L \rceilb=⌈log2​L⌉.

(a) Δ=0.1\Delta = 0.1Δ=0.1:

L=1+12.70.1=1+127=128L = 1 + \frac{12.7}{0.1} = 1 + 127 = 128L=1+0.112.7​=1+127=128 128=27  ⇒  b=7 bits128 = 2^7 \;\Rightarrow\; b = 7 \text{ bits}128=27⇒b=7 bits

(b) Δ=0.02\Delta = 0.02Δ=0.02:

L=1+12.70.02=1+635=636L = 1 + \frac{12.7}{0.02} = 1 + 635 = 636L=1+0.0212.7​=1+635=636 29=512<636≤1024=2102^9 = 512 < 636 \le 1024 = 2^{10}29=512<636≤1024=210 b=⌈log⁡2636⌉=⌈9.31⌉=10 bitsb = \lceil \log_2 636 \rceil = \lceil 9.31 \rceil = 10 \text{ bits}b=⌈log2​636⌉=⌈9.31⌉=10 bits

So a 7-bit A/D converter is enough for Δ=0.1\Delta = 0.1Δ=0.1, and a 10-bit A/D converter is needed for Δ=0.02\Delta = 0.02Δ=0.02.

Traps

  • Always round the bits up. 9.31 bits means 9 bits are not enough, so the answer is 10.
  • Keep the “+1”. Here it does not change the answers (127 levels also need 7 bits, and 635 also need 10), but it can. A range of 12.8 with Δ=0.1\Delta = 0.1Δ=0.1 has 128 gaps, so 129 levels and 8 bits, not 7.
  • Some books use Δ=(xmax−xmin)/2b\Delta = (x_{max} - x_{min})/2^bΔ=(xmax​−xmin​)/2b, which gives log⁡2127=6.99→7\log_2 127 = 6.99 \to 7log2​127=6.99→7 and log⁡2635=9.31→10\log_2 635 = 9.31 \to 10log2​635=9.31→10: the same answers. Proakis uses L−1L - 1L−1, so write that.

Bonus: check it in Python

import numpy as np
rng = 6.35 - (-6.35)   # 12.7
for D in (0.1, 0.02):
    # round(): 12.7/0.1 gives
    # 126.99999... in floats
    L = 1 + round(rng / D)
    b = int(np.ceil(np.log2(L)))
    print(D, L, b)
# 0.1 128 7
# 0.02 636 10

Check yourself

1. The same signal with Δ=0.05\Delta = 0.05Δ=0.05. How many bits?

L=1+12.7/0.05=1+254=255L = 1 + 12.7/0.05 = 1 + 254 = 255L=1+12.7/0.05=1+254=255. Since 28=256≥2552^8 = 256 \ge 25528=256≥255, 8 bits.

2. x(n)=cos⁡(πn/4)x(n) = \cos(\pi n/4)x(n)=cos(πn/4) with Δ=0.01\Delta = 0.01Δ=0.01. How many bits?

It reaches +1+1+1 at n=0n = 0n=0 and −1-1−1 at n=4n = 4n=4, so the range is 2. L=1+2/0.01=201L = 1 + 2/0.01 = 201L=1+2/0.01=201, and 27=128<201≤256=282^7 = 128 < 201 \le 256 = 2^827=128<201≤256=28, so 8 bits.

3. Why does the frequency π/10\pi/10π/10 not change the answer?

The number of bits depends only on the amplitude range and Δ\DeltaΔ. The frequency matters for sampling, not for quantization.

Session 6 · about 15 min · ★ asked twice, newest topic

Converting a digital signal back to analog

Asked: “Explain / sketch the process for converting a digital signal to its analog equivalent (with figure).” F22TT1NEW

Picture

The idea

The D/A converter has bits, and it wants a continuous signal that passes through the sample values. Filling in the signal between the samples is called interpolation.

  • Decoder. It turns each bbb-bit code back into its level, a voltage xq(n)x_q(n)xq​(n).
  • Sample-and-hold (zero-order hold). It keeps each value constant for TTT seconds, until the next one arrives. The result is a staircase. This is the simplest interpolator, and it is what most real D/A converters do.
  • Smoothing low-pass filter. The sharp corners of the staircase are high frequencies that were not in the original signal. In the spectrum they are the copies at ±Fs,±2Fs,…\pm F_s, \pm 2F_s, \dots±Fs​,±2Fs​,…, called images. An analog low-pass filter with cutoff near Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2 removes them, which rounds off the steps and leaves a smooth xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t). It is called the anti-imaging or reconstruction filter.

The ideal interpolator. The sampling theorem says that if Fs>2FmaxF_s > 2F_{max}Fs​>2Fmax​, the signal can be rebuilt exactly by placing a sinc pulse on every sample and adding them up:

xa(t)=∑n=−∞∞x(n) g(t−nT)x_a(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x(n)\, g(t - nT)xa​(t)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)g(t−nT) g(t)=sin⁡(πt/T)πt/Tg(t) = \frac{\sin(\pi t/T)}{\pi t/T}g(t)=πt/Tsin(πt/T)​

Each sinc pulse stretches forever in both directions, so this cannot be built exactly. Real converters approximate it with a zero-order hold followed by the smoothing filter, or with linear interpolation, which joins the samples with straight lines.

Write this in the exam

Draw the chain: digital signal (bits) → Decoder → sample values → Sample-and-hold (zero-order hold) → staircase → Smoothing (anti-imaging) low-pass filter → analog signal. Under it, sketch the samples, the staircase, and the smooth output. Then write:

Converting a digital signal to analog is a process of interpolation: the values between the samples must be filled in. The decoder converts each binary code word into a voltage level. The sample-and-hold, acting as a zero-order hold, holds each value constant for one sampling interval TTT, which gives a staircase approximation of the signal. The staircase contains unwanted high-frequency components (images of the spectrum at multiples of FsF_sFs​), so it is passed through an analog low-pass smoothing filter with cutoff Fs/2F_s/2Fs​/2, which gives the analog signal xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t).

The ideal D/A converter would use the ideal interpolation formula

xa(t)=∑n=−∞∞x(n) sin⁡[π(t−nT)/T]π(t−nT)/Tx_a(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x(n)\, \frac{\sin\left[\pi(t - nT)/T\right]}{\pi(t - nT)/T}xa​(t)=n=−∞∑∞​x(n)π(t−nT)/Tsin[π(t−nT)/T]​

but the sinc pulse is infinitely long, so in practice it is approximated by a zero-order hold (or linear interpolation) followed by a low-pass filter.

Bonus: why the staircase is not as bad as it looks

The zero-order hold has frequency response H(F)=T sin⁡(πFT)πFT e−jπFTH(F) = T\,\dfrac{\sin(\pi F T)}{\pi F T}\,e^{-j\pi F T}H(F)=TπFTsin(πFT)​e−jπFT. That is already a low-pass shape, so it weakens the images, and the smoothing filter finishes the job.

Check yourself

1. Why does the staircase need a filter after it?

Its sudden jumps contain high-frequency images at multiples of FsF_sFs​ that were not in the original signal. The low-pass filter removes them.

2. Why is the ideal sinc interpolator not used?

Each sinc pulse lasts from −∞-\infty−∞ to ∞\infty∞, so it would need every past and future sample. It cannot be built.

3. Can a D/A converter give back exactly the original analog signal?

No. Even a perfect interpolator only rebuilds the quantized samples, so the quantization error stays.

Session 7 · about 12 min

SQNR: definition, formula, and how to change it

Asked: “Define SQNR; how to reduce SQNR.” F22

The idea

SQNR stands for signal-to-quantization-noise ratio. It compares how strong the signal is with how strong the quantization error is. Think of the error eq(n)e_q(n)eq​(n) as a small noise added to the signal; then

SQNR=PxPq\text{SQNR} = \frac{P_x}{P_q}SQNR=Pq​Px​​

where PxP_xPx​ is the average power of the signal and PqP_qPq​ is the average power of the quantization noise. In decibels:

SQNR (dB)=10log⁡10PxPq\text{SQNR (dB)} = 10\log_{10}\frac{P_x}{P_q}SQNR (dB)=10log10​Pq​Px​​

A large SQNR means the quantization noise is small compared with the signal, which is what you want.

The formula for a sinusoid. Take a sinusoid of amplitude AAA that fills the whole range of a bbb-bit quantizer.

  1. The range is 2A2A2A and there are 2b2^b2b levels, so Δ=2A/2b\Delta = 2A/2^bΔ=2A/2b.
  2. The noise power is Pq=Δ212=A2/322bP_q = \dfrac{\Delta^2}{12} = \dfrac{A^2/3}{2^{2b}}Pq​=12Δ2​=22bA2/3​.
  3. The power of a sinusoid of amplitude AAA is Px=A2/2P_x = A^2/2Px​=A2/2.
SQNR=PxPq=A2/2A2/(3⋅22b)=32⋅22b\text{SQNR} = \frac{P_x}{P_q} = \frac{A^2/2}{A^2/(3\cdot 2^{2b})} = \frac{3}{2}\cdot 2^{2b}SQNR=Pq​Px​​=A2/(3⋅22b)A2/2​=23​⋅22b SQNR (dB)=10log⁡10SQNR=1.76+6.02 b dB\begin{aligned} \text{SQNR (dB)} &= 10\log_{10}\text{SQNR} \\ &= 1.76 + 6.02\,b \ \text{dB} \end{aligned}SQNR (dB)​=10log10​SQNR=1.76+6.02b dB​

So each extra bit adds about 6 dB. (16 bits is CD audio.)

Bits bbb81216
SQNR49.9 dB74.0 dB98.1 dB

About the wording “reduce SQNR”

You almost never want to reduce SQNR: a higher SQNR means less quantization noise. Write one line that shows you noticed (“SQNR is reduced by using fewer bits, that is a larger Δ\DeltaΔ; in practice we want to increase it, which is done by …”), then give the list below.

How to increase SQNR (that is, reduce the quantization noise)

  1. Use more bits. Each extra bit adds about 6.02 dB.
  2. Use the full range of the quantizer. The formula assumes the signal fills the range. A signal that uses only half the range loses about 6 dB, so amplify or scale it before the A/D converter, without letting it clip.
  3. Use non-uniform quantization (companding), such as μ-law or A-law, which keeps the SQNR high for quiet parts of the signal.
  4. Bonus: oversampling with noise shaping (sigma-delta converters) pushes the noise outside the signal band.

Write this in the exam

The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is the ratio of the average power of the signal to the average power of the quantization noise:

SQNR=PxPq\text{SQNR} = \frac{P_x}{P_q}SQNR=Pq​Px​​ SQNR (dB)=10log⁡10PxPq\text{SQNR (dB)} = 10\log_{10}\frac{P_x}{P_q}SQNR (dB)=10log10​Pq​Px​​

For a uniform quantizer with rounding, Pq=Δ2/12P_q = \Delta^2/12Pq​=Δ2/12. For a full-scale sinusoid quantized with bbb bits, SQNR=32⋅22b\text{SQNR} = \frac{3}{2}\cdot 2^{2b}SQNR=23​⋅22b, that is SQNR (dB)=1.76+6.02 b\text{SQNR (dB)} = 1.76 + 6.02\,bSQNR (dB)=1.76+6.02b. Each additional bit increases the SQNR by about 6 dB.

SQNR falls if fewer bits (a larger Δ\DeltaΔ) are used. To improve it: increase the number of bits, make the signal use the full range of the quantizer, or use non-uniform quantization (companding).

Bonus: where Δ2/12\Delta^2/12Δ2/12 comes from

With rounding, the error is equally likely to be anywhere between −Δ/2-\Delta/2−Δ/2 and Δ/2\Delta/2Δ/2. Its mean square value is

Pq=1Δ∫−Δ/2Δ/2e2 de=1Δ⋅e33∣−Δ/2Δ/2=Δ212\begin{aligned} P_q &= \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2\,de \\ &= \frac{1}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{e^3}{3}\Big|_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} = \frac{\Delta^2}{12} \end{aligned}Pq​​=Δ1​∫−Δ/2Δ/2​e2de=Δ1​⋅3e3​​−Δ/2Δ/2​=12Δ2​​

1.76+6.02×10=61.96≈621.76 + 6.02 \times 10 = 61.96 \approx 621.76+6.02×10=61.96≈62 dB.

2. You need at least 80 dB. How many bits?

b≥(80−1.76)/6.02=12.997b \ge (80 - 1.76)/6.02 = 12.997b≥(80−1.76)/6.02=12.997, so 13 bits. Check: 1.76+6.02×13=80.021.76 + 6.02 \times 13 = 80.021.76+6.02×13=80.02 dB.

3. Going from 8 bits to 16 bits improves the SQNR by how much?

8×6.02≈488 \times 6.02 \approx 488×6.02≈48 dB.

Sketch: 10 Hz sampled at 20 Hz

Asked: “Sketch the analog signal xa(t)x_a(t)xa​(t) of 10 Hz and its discrete-time equivalent sampled at 20 Hz.” TT1

Picture

The idea

  • The period is 1/10=0.11/10 = 0.11/10=0.1 s, and the sampling interval is T=1/20=0.05T = 1/20 = 0.05T=1/20=0.05 s, so there are exactly two samples in every period.
  • The digital frequency is f=F/Fs=10/20=1/2f = F/F_s = 10/20 = 1/2f=F/Fs​=10/20=1/2, so x(n)=cos⁡(2π⋅12n)=cos⁡(πn)=(−1)nx(n) = \cos(2\pi \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} n) = \cos(\pi n) = (-1)^nx(n)=cos(2π⋅21​n)=cos(πn)=(−1)n. The samples go 1,−1,1,−1,…1, -1, 1, -1, \dots1,−1,1,−1,…, with period N=2N = 2N=2. This is the fastest a discrete-time signal can oscillate: f=1/2f = 1/2f=1/2 is the highest digital frequency there is.
  • Here Fs=2FF_s = 2FFs​=2F exactly, which is right on the Nyquist rate. A cosine happens to be caught at its peaks, which is lucky. A sine at the same rate is caught at its zero crossings, so x(n)=sin⁡(πn)=0x(n) = \sin(\pi n) = 0x(n)=sin(πn)=0 for every nnn, and the signal disappears completely. Any other starting phase gives something in between. This is why the sampling theorem needs Fs>2FmaxF_s > 2F_{max}Fs​>2Fmax​, strictly greater.

A 3 Hz sine, the sampling rate, and the system function

Asked: “Draw a sine wave of F=3F = 3F=3 Hz. What is sampling rate? What is a system function? How can quantization error be reduced?” TT1

Picture

The idea, part by part

The sine wave. xa(t)=Asin⁡(2π⋅3t)x_a(t) = A\sin(2\pi \cdot 3t)xa​(t)=Asin(2π⋅3t). Its period is 1/31/31/3 s (about 0.333 s), so it completes three cycles every second. It starts at 0 going up, peaks at t=1/12t = 1/12t=1/12 s, crosses 0 at 1/61/61/6 s, reaches its lowest point at 1/41/41/4 s, and is back at 0 at 1/31/31/3 s.

Sampling rate. The sampling rate (sampling frequency) FsF_sFs​ is the number of samples taken per second, Fs=1/TF_s = 1/TFs​=1/T, where TTT is the time between samples. Its unit is hertz, meaning samples per second. To sample this 3 Hz sine without aliasing you need Fs>2×3=6F_s > 2 \times 3 = 6Fs​>2×3=6 Hz; 6 Hz is its Nyquist rate. For example, Fs=12F_s = 12Fs​=12 Hz gives

x(n)=Asin⁡(2π⋅312 n)=Asin⁡(πn2)={0, A, 0, −A, 0, A, … }\begin{aligned} x(n) &= A\sin\left(2\pi \cdot \tfrac{3}{12}\, n\right) = A\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi n}{2}\right) \\ &= \{0,\ A,\ 0,\ -A,\ 0,\ A,\ \dots\} \end{aligned}x(n)​=Asin(2π⋅123​n)=Asin(2πn​)={0, A, 0, −A, 0, A, …}​

That repeats every N=4N = 4N=4 samples.

System function. The system function of an LTI system is the z-transform of its impulse response h(n)h(n)h(n). It is also the ratio of the z-transforms of the output and the input:

H(z)=∑n=−∞∞h(n) z−n=Y(z)X(z)H(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(n)\,z^{-n} = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}H(z)=n=−∞∑∞​h(n)z−n=X(z)Y(z)​

For a system described by the difference equation y(n)=−∑k=1Nak y(n−k)+∑k=0Mbk x(n−k)y(n) = -\sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k\, y(n-k) + \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\, x(n-k)y(n)=−∑k=1N​ak​y(n−k)+∑k=0M​bk​x(n−k), it is a ratio of two polynomials in z−1z^{-1}z−1:

H(z)=∑k=0Mbk z−k1+∑k=1Nak z−kH(z) = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\, z^{-k}}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k\, z^{-k}}H(z)=1+∑k=1N​ak​z−k∑k=0M​bk​z−k​

For example, y(n)=0.5 y(n−1)+x(n)y(n) = 0.5\,y(n-1) + x(n)y(n)=0.5y(n−1)+x(n) gives H(z)=11−0.5z−1H(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.5z^{-1}}H(z)=1−0.5z−11​, with ROC ∣z∣>0.5\lvert z \rvert > 0.5∣z∣>0.5. Its poles and zeros describe the system completely, and evaluating it on the unit circle, z=ejωz = e^{j\omega}z=ejω, gives the frequency response H(ω)H(\omega)H(ω). (For an analog system the same idea uses the Laplace transform: H(s)=Y(s)/X(s)H(s) = Y(s)/X(s)H(s)=Y(s)/X(s).)

Reducing quantization error. This is the list from Session 4: more bits (a smaller Δ\DeltaΔ), rounding instead of truncation, a signal that fills the quantizer’s range without clipping, and non-uniform quantization (companding).

Write this in the exam

  1. Sketch xa(t)=Asin⁡(2π⋅3t)x_a(t) = A\sin(2\pi \cdot 3t)xa​(t)=Asin(2π⋅3t), period 1/31/31/3 s, three cycles in one second (sketch (a)).
  2. Sampling rate FsF_sFs​ is the number of samples taken per second, Fs=1/TF_s = 1/TFs​=1/T samples/s (Hz). By the sampling theorem it must be greater than twice the highest frequency, so here Fs>6F_s > 6Fs​>6 Hz. With Fs=12F_s = 12Fs​=12 Hz, x(n)=Asin⁡(πn/2)x(n) = A\sin(\pi n/2)x(n)=Asin(πn/2) (sketch (b)).
  3. System function H(z)H(z)H(z) is the z-transform of the impulse response, H(z)=∑h(n)z−n=Y(z)/X(z)H(z) = \sum h(n) z^{-n} = Y(z)/X(z)H(z)=∑h(n)z−n=Y(z)/X(z). For a difference equation it is the ratio ∑bkz−k/(1+∑akz−k)\sum b_k z^{-k} / (1 + \sum a_k z^{-k})∑bk​z−k/(1+∑ak​z−k).
  4. Quantization error is reduced by using more bits (smaller step Δ\DeltaΔ), rounding, using the quantizer’s full range, and companding.

Check yourself

1. What is the system function of y(n)=x(n)+x(n−1)y(n) = x(n) + x(n-1)y(n)=x(n)+x(n−1)?

H(z)=1+z−1H(z) = 1 + z^{-1}H(z)=1+z−1.

2. A 3 Hz sine is sampled at 4 Hz. What frequency do the samples show?

4 Hz is less than 6 Hz, so it aliases: 3−4=−13 - 4 = -13−4=−1, which looks like a 1 Hz sinusoid.

That is every question. Last stop: the Doomsday sheet.
